14cxkmj:133: : Splitting eval into an optimization set (to discover problems and propose changes) and a held-out set (to verify the generalization of changes on unseen samples) is standard practice. Optimization set improving + held-out set worsening means the Agent is "brushing familiar questions" without real generalization. Teams should establish a clear "held-out set pass rate" as the criterion for whether optimization is effective, to avoid mistaking overfitting for progress.

186bwsx:170: : Failure traces generated by real user usage have the highest behavioral authenticity—every failure trace is a naturally formed eval sample. Compared to manual curation (high value but hard to scale) and external datasets (only suitable as raw material), production traces provide the best balance of quality and scale. Teams should build an automated pipeline from production traces to evals to achieve scalable eval production.

These problems are essentially not behavioral signals that eval can capture, but judgments at the product experience level. Automated processes can exclude most common errors, but the final gate for product experience still requires human judgment.
1dtd85p:159: : The key insight from LangChain experiments is that many Agent failures are not because they "can't do the task", but because "the action rhythm is wrong". This means the focus of trace analysis should shift from "whether the final result is correct" to "whether the behavior sequence in the process is reasonable"—timing of tool selection, timing of search stopping, order of confirmation and execution, etc. Rhythm problems are more subtle than result problems, but easier to correct directionally through trace.

1jf2wm3:221: In LangChain's six-step method, the step of "splitting an optimization set and a held-out set" reveals the most overlooked overfitting problem in automatic optimization: if you repeatedly tune only on the optimization set, the Agent will eventually "memorize the questions" rather than truly improve its ability. The deep reason for this problem is that eval samples are themselves part of the Agent's training data—repeatedly adjusting the harness on the same batch of evals essentially teaches the Agent to "flatter" the surface features of these specific samples, rather than to master the general capabilities behind the task. The existence of a held-out set is essentially a defense mechanism against this data leakage.
1n74dvj:24: The held-out set is a necessary mechanism to prevent self-deception and should be used in every optimization iteration
1u33y0o:277: The design of the eval production flywheel reveals a positive feedback loop for capability evolution: more usage → more traces → more evals → better harness. The core driving force of this flywheel is the failure patterns contained in traces—every Agent failure trace is a potential source of eval. This means the quality of eval is directly proportional to trace coverage, and trace coverage is proportional to the scale of Agent usage. For teams just starting out, the early stage of the flywheel naturally faces a "chicken-or-egg" dilemma: without enough usage, there are not enough failure traces; without enough failure traces, high-quality evals cannot be built.

l1xjsa:239: The value of trace as a diagnostic tool far exceeds the superficial function of "recording the execution process". In Better-Harness methodology, trace is the only means to locate "action-rhythm problems"—when the Agent should stop but keeps searching, should act but repeatedly confirms, should ask about the goal but asks about implementation details. These vague behavioral anomalies can only be concretely located in trace. However, the value of trace depends on its granularity and readability: overly sparse trace cannot support targeted analysis, and overly dense trace causes information overload. In practice, teams need to find a balance between recording cost and analysis needs.

The behavioral label system of eval (whether search stops at the right time, tool selection, multi-step reasoning, etc.) is the foundation for building a behavioral map.

w240c0:249: Karpathy's Autoresearch proves automatic optimization "can run", but Better-Harness reveals the harder half: when the evaluation signal (eval) is wrong, the system will "run faster" in the wrong direction. The root of this core contradiction is that the relationship between eval and prompt/tools/workflow is essentially different from the relationship between test answers and programs—eval is a directional signal, and once the direction deviates, the optimization process accumulates wrong progress in the wrong direction. In traditional ML, gradient backpropagation can instantly correct direction errors, but harness optimization relies on discrete behavioral signals and cannot provide a similar instant correction mechanism.
